drills.q: What's the practical difference between a native <button> and a <div role="button">, and what's the minimum needed to make the div fully equivalent?
drills.a: A native button is focusable, fires click on Enter and Space, reports role:button, and participates in forms automatically. A div needs role="button", tabindex="0", a keydown handler for both Enter and Space, and an accessible name (visible text, aria-label, or aria-labelledby) -- worth asking why a real button couldn't be used instead.

drills.q: Explain precisely why "no ARIA is better than bad ARIA" is true rather than just a slogan, with a concrete example.
drills.a: ARIA only changes the accessibility tree, never actual browser behavior. A custom dropdown with role="listbox" and aria-expanded but no arrow-key navigation announces standard listbox behavior a screen reader user then expects and doesn't get -- more confusing than an unstyled list with no such claim.

drills.q: Walk through everything an accessible modal needs to do around focus, in order, and explain what breaks if you skip restoring focus on close.
drills.a: Move focus in on open, trap focus inside (Tab/Shift+Tab wrap at boundaries), close on Escape, restore focus to the trigger on close. Skipping the restore step leaves focus on body/a removed node, so a keyboard user has no idea where they are and must re-navigate from the top of the page -- invisible to mouse-driven QA.

drills.q: Why is a visually obvious form validation error sometimes completely silent to a screen reader, and when should you use aria-live="assertive" vs "polite"?
drills.a: Content injected with no aria-live ancestor and no focus movement produces no announcement -- screen readers announce on navigation/focus or inside a live region, not on DOM mutation alone. polite waits for current activity to finish (most updates); assertive interrupts immediately (reserve for genuinely urgent things like session expiry) since overuse of assertive is disorienting.

drills.q: Why does SPA client-side routing break something multi-page sites got for free, and what's the minimum fix?
drills.a: A full page load resets focus and announces the new title as a side effect; a client-side route change does neither automatically, so focus silently stays wherever it was and screen reader users get no signal navigation happened. Fix: move focus to the new page's <h1 tabIndex={-1}> and update document.title on route change.

drills.q: What does axe-core actually catch versus structurally miss, and is manual testing optional under time pressure?
drills.a: Catches structural/presence issues (missing alt text, contrast against computed styles, missing labels, invalid ARIA values) -- roughly 57% of WCAG issues on average. Misses whether behavior matches announced semantics, whether flows make sense read aloud, etc. Not fully optional if real usability matters, but prioritizable: automated on every PR as a floor, manual passes scheduled on high-risk flows (checkout, auth, nav).

drills.q: Explain WCAG's three conformance levels and why AAA isn't the target most teams should pursue, but note when selective AAA adoption makes sense.
drills.a: A = floor (unusable-if-missing, e.g. keyboard operability). AA = practical/legal target (4.5:1 contrast, visible focus, consistent nav) referenced by ADA case law, Section 508, EN 301 549. AAA (7:1 contrast, etc.) isn't W3C-recommended as a universal target since cost/benefit doesn't scale the same way across a whole product. Selective AAA adoption makes sense for a known specific need, e.g. higher contrast for a data-dense dashboard used by an older user base.

drills.q: A custom Select component passes every automated accessibility check but a user reports it's unusable with a screen reader. What's your diagnostic process, and what else could explain it if your own keyboard test works fine?
drills.a: Test keyboard-only (Tab reachability, arrow keys per ARIA APG listbox/combobox pattern, Enter/Space/Escape) and with an actual screen reader (VoiceOver/NVDA), checking that announced role/state changes match visual behavior -- automated tools verify markup, not live behavior correctness. If your own test passes, check screen-reader+browser combination specifics (VoiceOver/Safari, NVDA/Firefox, JAWS/Chrome have known quirks) and whether the bug depends on how focus arrived at the component.

drills.q: Why might color contrast pass for a default theme but fail in dark mode, and how would you prevent this systemically rather than catching it after the fact?
drills.a: Contrast is a function of the specific foreground/background pair; a token often gets manually verified only against the default (light) theme, and a dark-mode pairing introduces a new combination that can fall under AA thresholds unnoticed. Prevent it by baking automated contrast validation into the design-token pipeline/CI, checking every semantic color-pair across every defined theme, rather than relying on manual spot-checks.

drills.q: Give a real example where adding ARIA actively made a component worse than having none, and explain the general lesson.
drills.a: A dropdown given role="listbox" and aria-expanded purely to satisfy an automated scanner, but with no arrow-key navigation or Enter-to-select implemented -- a screen reader announces standard listbox affordances that then fail to work when the user tries them, which is more confusing than an unstyled list creating no such expectation. General lesson: ARIA is a claim about behavior, and an unfulfilled claim is worse than no claim, since it actively misleads rather than leaving an honest gap.
